11  I.   SUMMARY                                                         
12       Plaintiff Stratcomms LLC alleges that Defendant Republic of Mali breached a 
13  contract to pay Plaintiff in full for its consulting services and that Defendant has been 
14  unjustly enriched by Plaintiff’s services. (ECF No. 1 (“Complaint”).) Before the Court is 
15  Plaintiff’s motion for default judgment. (ECF No. 26 (“Motion”).) As explained below, the 
16  Court will grant the Motion as to Plaintiff’s breach of contract claim and deny the Motion 
17  as to Plaintiff’s unjust enrichment claim.                           
18  II.  DISCUSSION                                                      
19       The Court first addresses whether Plaintiff has met the procedural requirements 
20  for default judgment and whether the Court has jurisdiction over Plaintiff’s claims under 
21  the  Foreign  Sovereign  Immunities  Act  (“FSIA”).  The  Court  then  addresses  whether 
22  Plaintiff has satisfied the factors for obtaining default judgment articulated in Eitel v. 
23  McCool, 782 F.2d 1470, 1471-72 (9th Cir. 1986), and met the standard for obtaining 
24  default judgment against a foreign state under 28 U.S.C. § 1608(e).  
25       A.   Procedural Requirements                                    
26       Plaintiff has satisfied the procedural requirements for default judgment under Fed. 
27  R. Civ. P. 55(b). The Clerk of Court properly entered a default against Defendant under 
28                                                                       
2   served. (ECF No. 25.)                                                
3        B.   Jurisdiction                                               
4        “The FSIA is the sole basis of subject matter jurisdiction over suits involving foreign 
5   states and their agencies and instrumentalities.” Phaneuf v. Republic of Indonesia, 106 
6   F.3d 302, 304 (9th Cir. 1997) (citation omitted). “Under the FSIA, foreign states are 
7   immune from suit unless one of the enumerated exceptions to the Act applies.” Id. (citing 
8   28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1604-05). Under 28 U.S.C. § 1605(a)(2), “[a] foreign state shall not 
9   be immune from the jurisdiction of courts of the United States or of the States in any case 
10   . . . in which the action is based upon a commercial activity carried on in the United States 
11   by the foreign state.” Plaintiff asserts that Defendant is not entitled to immunity under § 
12   1605(a)(2) because “this action involves ‘commercial activity carried on in the United 
13   States by the foreign state’ – specifically, [D]efendant’s contracting for [P]laintiff, a U.S. 
14   entity, to perform services in the United States for [D]efendant’s economic benefit.” (ECF 
15   No. 1 at 2.) The Court agrees.                                       
16        Under  §  1603(d),  “[a]  ‘commercial  activity’  means  either  a  regular  course  of 
17   commercial conduct or a particular commercial transaction or act,” and “[t]he commercial 
18   character of an activity shall be determined by reference to the nature of the course of 
19   conduct or particular transaction or act, rather than by reference to its purpose.” Under § 
20   1603(e), “[a] ‘commercial activity carried on in the United States by a foreign state’ means 
21   commercial activity carried on by such state and having substantial contact with the 
22   United States.” “Even if performed with a public purpose in mind, acts by governmental 
23   entities are considered commercial in nature if the role of the sovereign is one that could 
24   be played by a private actor.” Park v. Shin, 313 F.3d 1138, 1145 (9th Cir. 2002). “Thus, 
25   an activity is commercial unless it is one that only a sovereign state could perform.” Id. 
26   The Ninth Circuit in Park noted examples of “a contract to purchase military supplies” and 
27   “[a]  government’s  issuance  of  bonds  in  order  to  refinance  government  debt”  as 
28   commercial in nature and subject to the “commercial activity exception.” See id.  
2   based LLC—for Plaintiff’s “consulting services for improving and strengthening relations 
3   between the Republic of Mali and the United States of America in the areas of politics, 
4   economics, and strategy” for the calendar year of 2019 in exchange for payment of 708 
5   million CFA francs (the “Contract”). (ECF No. 1 at 3-4; ECF No. 26-1 at 3-4.) Such 
6   contracting could be performed by a private actor and considered “commercial activity 
7   carried on in the United States” by Defendant that has “substantial contact with the United 
8   States.” The Court therefore finds that the “commercial activity” exception to foreign 
9   sovereign immunity applies, and it has jurisdiction here.            
10        C.   Eitel Factors and 28 U.S.C. § 1608(e)                      
11        “The district court’s decision whether to enter a default judgment is a discretionary 
12   one.” Aldabe v. Aldabe, 616 F.2d 1089, 1092 (9th Cir. 1980). The Ninth Circuit has 
13   identified the following factors as relevant to the exercise of a court's discretion in 
14   determining whether to grant default judgment: (1) the possibility of prejudice to the 
15   plaintiff; (2) the merits of the plaintiff’s substantive claims; (3) the sufficiency of the 
16   complaint; (4) the sum of money at stake in the action; (5) the possibility of a dispute 
17   concerning material facts; (6) whether the default was due to excusable neglect; and (7) 
18   the strong policy underlying the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure favoring decisions on 
19   the merits. Eitel, 782 F.2d at 1471-72.                              
20        “[D]efault judgments against foreign nations are generally disfavored.” Doe v. Qi, 
21   349 F. Supp. 2d 1258, 1273 (N.D. Cal. 2004) (citing Restatement (Third) of Foreign 
22   Relations Law § 459 cmt c (1987)). “Courts have gone to considerable lengths to allow 
23   default judgments against foreign states to be set aside.” Id. (collecting cases). Under 28 
24   U.S.C. § 1608(e), “[n]o judgment by default shall be entered by a court of the United 
25   States or of a State against a foreign state, a political subdivision thereof, or an agency 
26   or instrumentality of a foreign state, unless the claimant establishes his claim or right to 
27   relief by evidence satisfactory to the court.”                       
28                                                                        
2   standard below.                                                      
3             1.   First, Fifth, Sixth, and Seventh Eitel Factors        
4        “In cases . . . in which the defendant has not participated in the litigation, the first, 
5   fifth, sixth, and seventh Eitel factors are easily satisfied.” Hygenix, LLC v. Xie, Case No. 
6   2:21-cv-00957-JAD-EJY, 2022 WL 1094181, at *1 (D. Nev. Apr. 11, 2022). Such is the 
7   case here. The first factor—the possibility of prejudice to the plaintiff—weighs in favor of 
8   granting default judgment because, if Plaintiff’s Motion is not granted, Plaintiff would likely 
9   be without other recourse for recovery and would suffer significant prejudice. The fifth and 
10   sixth factors—the possibility of a dispute concerning material facts and whether the 
11   default was due to the excusable neglect—also weigh in favor of default judgment. Due 
12   to Defendant’s failure to participate, there is no dispute over material facts and no 
13   indication that the default is due to excusable neglect. Lastly, while the seventh factor—
14   the strong policy favoring decisions on the merits—“arguably always weighs against the 
15   entry of default judgment because cases should be decided on their merits whenever 
16   reasonably possible,” “when defendants fail to answer the complaint, a decision on the 
17   merits is impractical, if not impossible.” See Hygenix, 2022 WL 1094181, at *1 (citations 
18   and internal quotations omitted). The seventh factor thus will not preclude the Court from 
19   entering default judgment.                                           
20             2.   Second and Third Eitel Factors                        
21        The second and third factors consider the merits of the plaintiff’s substantive claims 
22   and the sufficiency of the complaint. Eitel, 782 F.2d at 1471. “Of all the Eitel factors, courts 
23   often consider the second and third factors to be the most important.” See Hygenix, 2022 
24   WL 1094181, at *2 (citation omitted). Generally, “upon default the factual allegations of 
25   the complaint, except those relating to the amount of damages, will be taken as true.” 
26   TeleVideo Sys., Inc. v. Heidenthal, 826 F.2d 915, 917-18 (9th Cir. 1987). “However, 
27   necessary facts not contained in the pleadings, and claims which are legally insufficient, 
28   are not established by default.” Cripps v. Life Ins. Co. of N. Am., 980 F.2d 1261, 1267 
2   of contract and unjust enrichment claims.                            
3                  a.   Breach of Contract                               
4        Under Nevada law, “[t]o succeed on a breach of contract claim, a plaintiff must 
5   show four elements: (1) formation of a valid contract; (2) performance or excuse of 
6   performance by the plaintiff; (3) material breach by the defendant; and (4) damages.” 
7   Laguerre v. Nevada Sys. of Higher Educ., 837 F. Supp. 2d 1176, 1180 (D. Nev. 2011) 
8   (citing Bernard v. Rockhill Dev. Co., 734 P.2d 1238, 1240 (Nev. 1987)). Plaintiff alleges 
9   and  supports  with evidence  that  it entered  into  a  valid  contract  with  Defendant for 
10   Plaintiff’s  consulting  services  in  exchange  for  payment—the  Contract,  that  Plaintiff 
11   performed its obligations under the Contract, and that Defendant breached the Contract 
12   by failing to pay half of the agreed-upon payment, resulting in damages. (ECF No. 1 at 4-
13   8; ECF No. 26-6 at 3-6; ECF Nos. 26-1, 26-2, 26-3, 26-5.) The Court therefore finds that 
14   Plaintiff has sufficiently stated a breach of contract claim and demonstrated its merits. 
15   The second and third Eitel factors thus weigh in favor of default judgment as to the breach 
16   of contract claim.                                                   
17                  b.   Unjust Enrichment                                
18        Unjust enrichment is based on the doctrine of quasi-contract, and “[t]he essential 
19   elements of quasi[-]contract are a benefit conferred on the defendant by the plaintiff, 
20   appreciation by the defendant of such benefit, and acceptance and retention by the 
21   defendant of such benefit under circumstances such that it would be inequitable for him 
22   to retain the benefit without payment of the value thereof.” Unionamerica Mortg. & Equity 
23   Tr. v. McDonald, 626 P.2d 1272, 1273 (Nev. 1981) (citations omitted). “An action based 
24   on a theory of unjust enrichment is not available when there is an express, written 
25   contract, because no agreement can be implied when there is an express agreement.” 
26   Leasepartners Corp. v. Robert L. Brooks Tr. Dated Nov. 12, 1975, 942 P.2d 182, 187 
27   (Nev. 1997).                                                         
28                                                                        
2   substantial  benefits  from  Plaintiff’s  services,”  “Plaintiff  performed  such  services  at 
3   Defendant’s request and in reliance on promises that Defendant would pay for them,” and 
4   as a result of Plaintiff’s services in 2019, “Defendant received $93 million more in aid from 
5   the United States than it had before.” (ECF No. 1 at 8-9.) Plaintiff alleges that “[f]or 
6   refusing to recognize its obligations under the Contract . . . Defendant should have to 
7   disgorge to Plaintiff the benefits that Plaintiff’s services conferred.” (Id.)  
8        Plaintiff’s unjust enrichment claim is plainly based on the Contract—an express, 
9   written contract—and thus fails as a matter of law. See Leasepartners, 942 P.2d at 187. 
10   Plaintiff appears to have also pled the unjust enrichment claim in the alternative to the 
11   breach of contract claim “if and to the extent the Court finds the Contract unenforceable 
12   in whole or in part.” (ECF No. 1 at 8.) Because the Court finds that Plaintiff has established 
13   its breach of contract claim, it cannot find as viable Plaintiff’s alternative unjust enrichment 
14   claim based on the same factual allegations of services provided in 2019. 
15        To the extent Plaintiff now argues in its Motion that its unjust enrichment claim is 
16   based on the value of its work—allegedly $10 million a year—for obtaining continued U.S. 
17   aid at the 2019 levels for each of the subsequent three years (ECF No. 26 at 3, 15-16), 
18   the Court is not persuaded that default judgment is warranted. First, “[a] default judgment 
19   must not differ in kind from, or exceed in amount, what is demanded in the pleadings.” 
20   Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(c). Plaintiff is essentially asking for default judgment on its unjust 
21   enrichment claim based on alleged quasi-contracts formed and benefits conferred after 
22   2019 that were not pled in its Complaint. The Complaint does not even mention what 
23   Plaintiff now claims in its Motion—that the then Mali prime minister purportedly valued 
24   Plaintiff’s work of obtaining increased U.S. aid for Mali at $10 million a year and that Mali 
25   continued to receive U.S. aid at the 2019 levels in subsequent years (ECF No. 26 at 15-
26   16). Plaintiff cannot now request a default judgment that differs from what is demanded 
27   in the pleadings.                                                    
28                                                                        
2   a foreign state is particularly disfavored. Plaintiff argues that it would be unjust to allow 
3   Mali to retain the additional $93 million in U.S. aid for each of the last four years it received 
4   as a result of Plaintiff’s services because, after having undergone two military coups, Mali 
5   has  purportedly  used  such  funding  “contrary  to  the  purpose  for  which  the  U.S. 
6   government had provided it and, as such, against American interest.” (ECF No. 26 at 7, 
7   16.) Even assuming Plaintiff’s services could be fairly traced to the continued increased 
8   levels  of  funding,  such  matters  ultimately  concern  foreign  policy  interests  and 
9   appropriation decisions that implicate the executive and legislative branches of the U.S. 
10   government. The U.S. government presumably could have reduced its funding to Mali 
11   after the alleged installation of a “Moscow-backed military dictatorship that threatens . . . 
12   the interests of the United States” if it had chosen to do so. (ECF No. 26 at 3.) Even 
13   assuming Plaintiff could establish an unjust enrichment claim based on such allegations, 
14   the Court declines to interfere with those executive and legislative matters.  
15        The Court therefore finds that Plaintiff has failed to establish an unjust enrichment 
16   claim, and the second and third Eitel factors weigh against default judgment as to this 
17   claim.                                                               
18             3.   Fourth Eitel Factor                                   
19        The fourth Eitel factor concerns the sum of money at stake in the action. 782 F.2d 
20   at  1471.  “[T]he  Court  considers  the  amount  of  money  requested  in  relation  to  the 
21   seriousness of the defendant’s conduct, whether large sums of money are involved, and 
22   whether the recovery sought is proportional to the harm caused by [the] defendant's 
23   conduct.” Next Gaming, LLC v. Glob. Gaming Grp., Inc., Case No. 2:14-cv-00071-MMD-
24   CWH, 2016 WL 3750651, at *3 (D. Nev. July 13, 2016) (citations and internal quotations 
25   omitted). The Court addresses the damages requested for each of Plaintiff’s claims in 
26   turn.                                                                
27                                                                        
28                                                                        
2        For the breach of contract claim, Plaintiff seeks to recover “the remaining half of 
3   the consideration due under the Contract, which amounts to $588,675.48 at current 
4   exchange rates.” (ECF No. 26 at 14; ECF No. 1 at 9.) “The fundamental principle that 
5   underlies the availability of contract damages is that of compensation.” 24 Williston on 
6   Contracts § 64:1 (4th ed. 2023). The goal is to place the plaintiff “in as good a position as 
7   [they] would have occupied had the defendant-promisor not breached the contract,” so 
8   the plaintiff is “generally entitled to an award of money damages in an amount reasonably 
9   calculated to make [them] whole and neither more nor less.” Id. Because Plaintiff’s 
10   requested breach-of-contract damages are reasonable and proportionate to the harm 
11   suffered, this factor weighs in favor of default judgment in that amount.  
12        Plaintiff also requests, in cursory fashion, prejudgment interest on the breach-of-
13   contract damages calculated from January 1, 2020. (ECF No. 26 at 3, 16.) However, 
14   Plaintiff has provided no argument to demonstrate that it is entitled to interest on those 
15   damages, so the Court denies the request for interest.               
16                  b.   Unjust Enrichment                                
17        Plaintiff requests $30 million in damages for its unjust enrichment claim—$10 
18   million for each of at least three years of Defendant’s “misused gains” of an increase in 
19   $93 million a year of U.S. government funding. (Id. at 3, 17.) That “the amount of damages 
20   sought are significant” itself weighs against default judgment on this claim. See Lasheen 
21   v. Loomis Co., Case No. 2:01-cv-0227-LKK-EFB, 2013 WL 1178209, at *8 (E.D. Cal. Mar. 
22   21, 2013), report and recommendation adopted, Case No. 2:01-cv-0227-LKK-EFB, 2013 
23   WL 5375815 (E.D. Cal. Sept. 24, 2013), aff’d sub nom. Lasheen v. Embassy of The Arab 
24   Republic of Egypt, 625 F. App’x 338 (9th Cir. 2015), and amended, Case No. 2:01-cv-
25   00227-KJM-EFB, 2016 WL 4161119 (E.D. Cal. Aug. 4, 2016). In addition, the Court finds 
26   that the requested amount of damages is completely disproportionate and inappropriate 
27   given  that  Plaintiff’s  unjust  enrichment  claim  is  legally  insufficient  for  the  reasons 
28   discussed above and where Plaintiff will already be compensated in breach-of-contract 
2   damages are likely too speculative or attenuated based on the limited evidence Plaintiff 
3   proffered, and the awarding of such damages would unduly interfere with the conduct of 
4   the executive and legislative branches for the reasons discussed above. The fourth Eitel 
5   factor therefore weighs against default judgment on the unjust enrichment claim.  
6        Taken together, the Eitel factors weigh in favor of granting default judgment on the 
7   breach of contract claim, and the Court finds that Plaintiff has “establishe[d] [its] claim or 
8   right to relief by evidence satisfactory to the court” to warrant default judgment against 
9   Defendant on the breach of contract claim for $588,675.48 in damages. See 28 U.S.C. § 
10   1608(e). The Court will therefore grant default judgment on the breach of contract claim 
11   in that amount.                                                      
12        On the other hand, the most important Eitel factors and the Eitel factors as a whole 
13   weigh against granting default judgment on the unjust enrichment claim, and the Court 
14   finds that Plaintiff has failed to establish its claim or right to relief for unjust enrichment 
15   under 28 U.S.C. § 1608(e). The Court will therefore deny default judgment on the unjust 
16   enrichment claim.                                                    
17   III.  CONCLUSION                                                     
18        The Court notes that Plaintiff made several arguments and cited to several cases 
19   not  discussed  above.  The  Court  has  reviewed  these  arguments  and  cases  and 
20   determines that they do not warrant discussion as they do not affect the outcome of the 
21   motion before the Court.                                             
22        It is therefore ordered that Plaintiff Stratcomms LLC’s motion for default judgment 
23   (ECF No. 26) is granted in part and denied in part. It is granted as to the breach of contract 
24   claim and denied as to the unjust enrichment claim.                  
25        The Clerk of Court is directed to enter judgment in favor of Plaintiff and against 
26   Defendant for $588,675.48 on the breach of contract claim.           
27        The Clerk of Court is further directed to enter judgment in favor of Defendant and 
28   against Plaintiff on the unjust enrichment claim.                    
 1          The Clerk of Court is further directed to close this case. 
2          DATED THIS     Day of April 2024.

9   and  supports  with evidence  that  it entered  into  a  valid  contract  with  Defendant for 
10   Plaintiff’s  consulting  services  in  exchange  for  payment—the  Contract,  that  Plaintiff 
11   performed its obligations under the Contract, and that Defendant breached the Contract 
12   by failing to pay half of the agreed-upon payment, resulting in damages. (ECF No. 1 at 4-
13   8; ECF No. 26-6 at 3-6; ECF Nos. 26-1, 26-2, 26-3, 26-5.) The Court therefore finds that 
14   Plaintiff has sufficiently stated a breach of contract claim and demonstrated its merits. 
15   The second and third Eitel factors thus weigh in favor of default judgment as to the breach 
16   of contract claim.                                                   
17                  b.   Unjust Enrichment                                
18        Unjust enrichment is based on the doctrine of quasi-contract, and “[t]he essential 
19   elements of quasi[-]contract are a benefit conferred on the defendant by the plaintiff, 
20   appreciation by the defendant of such benefit, and acceptance and retention by the 
21   defendant of such benefit under circumstances such that it would be inequitable for him 
22   to retain the benefit without payment of the value thereof.” Unionamerica Mortg. & Equity 
23   Tr. v. McDonald,
626 P.2d 1272, 1273
 (Nev. 1981) (citations omitted). “An action based 
24   on a theory of unjust enrichment is not available when there is an express, written 
25   contract, because no agreement can be implied when there is an express agreement.” 
26   Leasepartners Corp. v. Robert L. Brooks Tr. Dated Nov. 12, 1975,
942 P.2d 182
, 187 
27   (Nev. 1997).                                                         
28                                                                        
2   substantial  benefits  from  Plaintiff’s  services,”  “Plaintiff  performed  such  services  at 
3   Defendant’s request and in reliance on promises that Defendant would pay for them,” and 
4   as a result of Plaintiff’s services in 2019, “Defendant received $93 million more in aid from 
5   the United States than it had before.” (ECF No. 1 at 8-9.) Plaintiff alleges that “[f]or 
6   refusing to recognize its obligations under the Contract . . . Defendant should have to 
7   disgorge to Plaintiff the benefits that Plaintiff’s services conferred.” (Id.)  
8        Plaintiff’s unjust enrichment claim is plainly based on the Contract—an express, 
9   written contract—and thus fails as a matter of law. See Leasepartners,
942 P.2d at 187
. 
10   Plaintiff appears to have also pled the unjust enrichment claim in the alternative to the 
11   breach of contract claim “if and to the extent the Court finds the Contract unenforceable 
12   in whole or in part.” (ECF No. 1 at 8.) Because the Court finds that Plaintiff has established 
13   its breach of contract claim, it cannot find as viable Plaintiff’s alternative unjust enrichment 
14   claim based on the same factual allegations of services provided in 2019. 
15        To the extent Plaintiff now argues in its Motion that its unjust enrichment claim is 
16   based on the value of its work—allegedly $10 million a year—for obtaining continued U.S. 
17   aid at the 2019 levels for each of the subsequent three years (ECF No. 26 at 3, 15-16), 
18   the Court is not persuaded that default judgment is warranted. First, “[a] default judgment 
19   must not differ in kind from, or exceed in amount, what is demanded in the pleadings.” 
20   Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(c). Plaintiff is essentially asking for default judgment on its unjust 
21   enrichment claim based on alleged quasi-contracts formed and benefits conferred after 
22   2019 that were not pled in its Complaint. The Complaint does not even mention what 
23   Plaintiff now claims in its Motion—that the then Mali prime minister purportedly valued 
24   Plaintiff’s work of obtaining increased U.S. aid for Mali at $10 million a year and that Mali 
25   continued to receive U.S. aid at the 2019 levels in subsequent years (ECF No. 26 at 15-
26   16). Plaintiff cannot now request a default judgment that differs from what is demanded 
27   in the pleadings.                                                    
28                                                                        
2   a foreign state is particularly disfavored. Plaintiff argues that it would be unjust to allow 
3   Mali to retain the additional $93 million in U.S. aid for each of the last four years it received 
4   as a result of Plaintiff’s services because, after having undergone two military coups, Mali 
5   has  purportedly  used  such  funding  “contrary  to  the  purpose  for  which  the  U.S. 
6   government had provided it and, as such, against American interest.” (ECF No. 26 at 7, 
7   16.) Even assuming Plaintiff’s services could be fairly traced to the continued increased 
8   levels  of  funding,  such  matters  ultimately  concern  foreign  policy  interests  and 
9   appropriation decisions that implicate the executive and legislative branches of the U.S. 
10   government. The U.S. government presumably could have reduced its funding to Mali 
11   after the alleged installation of a “Moscow-backed military dictatorship that threatens . . . 
12   the interests of the United States” if it had chosen to do so. (ECF No. 26 at 3.) Even 
13   assuming Plaintiff could establish an unjust enrichment claim based on such allegations, 
14   the Court declines to interfere with those executive and legislative matters.  
15        The Court therefore finds that Plaintiff has failed to establish an unjust enrichment 
16   claim, and the second and third Eitel factors weigh against default judgment as to this 
17   claim.                                                               
18             3.   Fourth Eitel Factor                                   
19        The fourth Eitel factor concerns the sum of money at stake in the action.
782 F.2d 20 at 1471
.  “[T]he  Court  considers  the  amount  of  money  requested  in  relation  to  the 
21   seriousness of the defendant’s conduct, whether large sums of money are involved, and 
22   whether the recovery sought is proportional to the harm caused by [the] defendant's 
23   conduct.” Next Gaming, LLC v. Glob. Gaming Grp., Inc., Case No. 2:14-cv-00071-MMD-
24   CWH,
2016 WL 3750651
, at *3 (D. Nev. July 13, 2016) (citations and internal quotations 
25   omitted). The Court addresses the damages requested for each of Plaintiff’s claims in 
26   turn.                                                                
27                                                                        
28                                                                        
2        For the breach of contract claim, Plaintiff seeks to recover “the remaining half of 
3   the consideration due under the Contract, which amounts to $588,675.48 at current 
4   exchange rates.” (ECF No. 26 at 14; ECF No. 1 at 9.) “The fundamental principle that 
5   underlies the availability of contract damages is that of compensation.” 24 Williston on 
6   Contracts § 64:1 (4th ed. 2023). The goal is to place the plaintiff “in as good a position as 
7   [they] would have occupied had the defendant-promisor not breached the contract,” so 
8   the plaintiff is “generally entitled to an award of money damages in an amount reasonably 
9   calculated to make [them] whole and neither more nor less.” Id. Because Plaintiff’s 
10   requested breach-of-contract damages are reasonable and proportionate to the harm 
11   suffered, this factor weighs in favor of default judgment in that amount.  
12        Plaintiff also requests, in cursory fashion, prejudgment interest on the breach-of-
13   contract damages calculated from January 1, 2020. (ECF No. 26 at 3, 16.) However, 
14   Plaintiff has provided no argument to demonstrate that it is entitled to interest on those 
15   damages, so the Court denies the request for interest.               
16                  b.   Unjust Enrichment                                
17        Plaintiff requests $30 million in damages for its unjust enrichment claim—$10 
18   million for each of at least three years of Defendant’s “misused gains” of an increase in 
19   $93 million a year of U.S. government funding. (Id. at 3, 17.) That “the amount of damages 
20   sought are significant” itself weighs against default judgment on this claim. See Lasheen 
21   v. Loomis Co., Case No. 2:01-cv-0227-LKK-EFB,
2013 WL 1178209
, at *8 (E.D. Cal. Mar. 
22   21, 2013), report and recommendation adopted, Case No. 2:01-cv-0227-LKK-EFB, 2013
23 WL 5375815
 (E.D. Cal. Sept. 24, 2013), aff’d sub nom. Lasheen v. Embassy of The Arab 
24   Republic of Egypt,
625 F. App’x 338
 (9th Cir. 2015), and amended, Case No. 2:01-cv-
25   00227-KJM-EFB,
2016 WL 4161119
 (E.D. Cal. Aug. 4, 2016). In addition, the Court finds 
26   that the requested amount of damages is completely disproportionate and inappropriate 
27   given  that  Plaintiff’s  unjust  enrichment  claim  is  legally  insufficient  for  the  reasons 
28   discussed above and where Plaintiff will already be compensated in breach-of-contract 
2   damages are likely too speculative or attenuated based on the limited evidence Plaintiff 
3   proffered, and the awarding of such damages would unduly interfere with the conduct of 
4   the executive and legislative branches for the reasons discussed above. The fourth Eitel 
5   factor therefore weighs against default judgment on the unjust enrichment claim.  
6        Taken together, the Eitel factors weigh in favor of granting default judgment on the 
7   breach of contract claim, and the Court finds that Plaintiff has “establishe[d] [its] claim or 
8   right to relief by evidence satisfactory to the court” to warrant default judgment against 
9   Defendant on the breach of contract claim for $588,675.48 in damages. See
28 U.S.C. § 10
   1608(e). The Court will therefore grant default judgment on the breach of contract claim 
11   in that amount.                                                      
12        On the other hand, the most important Eitel factors and the Eitel factors as a whole 
13   weigh against granting default judgment on the unjust enrichment claim, and the Court 
14   finds that Plaintiff has failed to establish its claim or right to relief for unjust enrichment 
15   under
28 U.S.C. § 1608
(e). The Court will therefore deny default judgment on the unjust 
16   enrichment claim.
